expected_evidence: Ice-core geochemical anomalies in Greenland cores (GISP2/GRIP/NEEM) at ~12,800 cal BP: platinum, iridium, or other siderophile-element spikes; ammonium and nitrate spikes consistent with a biomass-burning/combustion event
Ice-core ash/soot or black-carbon layer coincident with the Younger Dryas onset
Extraterrestrial impact markers in terrestrial sediment sequences (nanodiamonds, magnetic and glassy spherules, melt-glass) at the Younger Dryas Boundary layer across multiple continents
A 'black mat' organic-rich sedimentary layer overlying YDB sites, interpreted as evidence of ecosystem collapse/biomass burning
Continental-scale charcoal/PAH (combustion aerosol) spikes indicating widespread biomass burning ('impact winter' wildfires)
Archaeological evidence of population decline or discontinuity in Clovis-age (or contemporaneous Eurasian) sites immediately after ~10,850 BCE
Faunal extinction/turnover data (megafauna decline) clustering at the same horizon
Genetic bottleneck signatures in human mtDNA/Y-chromosome lineages or megafaunal genomes dated to this interval

Model-based climate/impact-winter simulations predicting global cooling and biomass-burning aerosol loading matching Younger Dryas onset dynamics (this is itself largely model-prior, not direct observation)
response.rationale: This hypothesis corresponds to the well-known (and still contested) Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH), with the -10,850 date sitting essentially at the Younger Dryas onset (~12,800 cal BP). Given the explicit place='greenland-ice-sheet', the most diagnostic evidence class is geological/ice-core chemistry: Greenland ice cores are continuous, annually-layered, and preserve chemical stratigraphy across this exact interval, so geological detectability is comparatively high (0.6–0.65 per the younger-dryas row) and is the category most likely to actually confirm or refute a synchronous impact/biomass-burning-winter signal (e.g., the debated platinum anomaly reported by Petaev et al. 2013 in GISP2). Astronomical evidence (extraterrestrial markers, spherules, nanodiamonds) also has high nominal detectability (0.7) because such markers are physically robust and have been searched for extensively at Younger Dryas Boundary sites worldwide, though their interpretation remains scientifically contested (many independent labs failed to replicate key YDB markers). Material/archaeological evidence for population-demography effects (Clovis decline, faunal turnover) has only moderate detectability (0.35) because continent-wide demographic collapse is hard to date precisely and confounded by other causes (climate, overhunting). Genetic evidence for a population bottleneck at this exact date is weakly detectable (0.3) given the low resolution and small sample sizes typical of Pleistocene-boundary genetic reconstructions. Textual evidence is essentially impossible (0.0, pre-writing) and oral-tradition/iconographic evidence is very low (0.1) given the ~12,800-year gap and lack of continuous transmission. Overall, because ice-core stratigraphy specifically (the named 'place') is exceptionally well-preserved and continuously sampled across exactly this interval, absence of a clear, reproducible geochemical/combustion signal in Greenland ice cores is reasonably strong evidence against the hypothesis rather than merely a detectability artifact — but the broader multi-proxy demographic and genetic claims are inherently harder to detect and their absence should not be read as strongly falsifying. I set the overall detectability adjustment at 0.55, roughly averaging the high-detectability geological/astronomical channels most relevant to the stated placement with the much lower-detectability demographic/genetic/textual channels the hypothesis also implicitly requires (population-demography outcome). This reflects that meaningful evidence could plausibly survive and has in fact been actively searched for by the scientific community (per model-prior, unverified against the evidence text provided), even though the hypothesis as a whole remains empirically contested.
